body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mindy Kaling loves Indian food but faces challenges with her kids' preferences.
  • She enjoys Indian cuisine during rare moments away from her children.
  • Kaling's relationship with food reflects her Tamil and Bengali heritage.
  • Food serves as a bridge to her late mother and cultural identity.
  • Her experiences resonate with many Indian-American parents navigating similar culinary challenges.
Mindy's Culinary Balancing Act
›Kaling is a mother of three, balancing her food preferences with her kids'.
›She often enjoys Indian food during solo meals or outings with friends.
›Kaling shares her love for Indian cuisine on social media.
›Her cooking experiences reflect her Tamil and Bengali heritage.

Mindy Kaling has never been shy about her love for Indian food. The Emmy-nominated actress, writer, and producer — known for The Office, The Mindy Project, and Never Have I Ever — has built a reputation as one of Hollywood’s most vocal champions of Indian cuisine. But as any parent of young children knows, enjoying a fiery plate of vindaloo or a perfectly spiced masala dosa is not always easy when your dinner companions prefer chicken nuggets and plain pasta.

The Guilty Pleasure of Solo Indian Dining

Kaling, a mother of three, has spoken candidly about the challenge of maintaining her deep connection to Indian food while navigating the culinary preferences of small children. Like many Indian-American parents, she finds herself straddling two worlds at the dinner table: the rich, complex flavors of her Tamil and Bengali heritage and the decidedly milder tastes that most young kids gravitate toward.

The solution, she has noted with characteristic humor, often involves enjoying her favorite Indian dishes during those rare, blissful moments away from her children — a solo lunch, a dinner with friends, or a quick takeout order that does not need to pass the picky-eater test. It is a sentiment that resonates deeply with first- and second-generation Indian-American parents who grew up eating their parents’ cooking and now find their own kids pushing away the chana masala.

A Lifelong Love Affair With Indian Cuisine

Kaling’s relationship with Indian food has been a consistent thread throughout her public life. She has shared her shortcut chana masala recipe on Instagram, famously made masala dosas with then-Senator Kamala Harris in a viral 2019 cooking video, and has been spotted enjoying South Indian fare at restaurants from Los Angeles to New York, including at Priyanka Chopra Jonas’s Manhattan restaurant Sona.

Her social media posts regularly feature Indian dishes — from coconut chutney paired with crispy dosas to elaborate thalis. “Dosa + Masala + Coconut Chutney + Tomato Chutney,” she once captioned an Instagram story, a simple equation that any South Indian food lover would recognize as perfection.

Food as Heritage

Culinary Heritage and Identity
›Food connects Kaling to her late mother, who emigrated from Chennai.
›Her show 'Never Have I Ever' explores Indian-American identity through food.
›Kaling defends Indian cuisine against cultural dismissals.
›Her experiences reflect a universal story within the Indian diaspora.

For Kaling, food has always been more than sustenance. It is a bridge to her late mother, Swati Chokalingam, who emigrated from Chennai, and to the Tamil culture that shaped her upbringing in Cambridge, Massachusetts. In her show Never Have I Ever, food serves as a recurring motif for the protagonist Devi’s negotiation between Indian and American identity — a tension Kaling has acknowledged drawing from her own life.

When Kaling defended Indian cuisine against a Washington Post columnist who infamously dismissed it as being based on “one spice,” her response was both pointed and personal: “You don’t like a cuisine? Fine. But it’s so weird to feel defiantly proud of not liking a cuisine.”

A Universal Diaspora Story

Kaling’s juggling act between her Indian food cravings and her kids’ palates mirrors a broader experience across the Indian diaspora. Whether it is a parent in Fremont sneaking off for a plate of gobi manchurian or a mother in Edison making two dinners — one for the adults, one for the children — the negotiation between heritage cuisine and kids’ comfort food is a familiar refrain. In sharing her own version of this story, Kaling makes the everyday comedy of diasporic parenting feel both seen and celebrated.
author: Diaspora Desk
